extracted.intended_audience: aspiring screenwriters, novelists, and graphic-novel writers seeking a practical story-structure template
extracted.subtask_description: A concise, how-to summary of Blake Snyder's 'Save the Cat' beat sheet: a bite-size breakdown of three-act story structure into named beats with specific goals, examples, and usage notes for applying the template to screenplays, novels, and graphic novels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Overall: Beat Sheet purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: The Blake Snyder Beat Sheet is the best plot structure template; it breaks down the three-act structure into bite-size, manageable sections, each with a specific goal for your overall story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the Beat Sheet as a practical template to map story beats and ensure each section advances plot and theme. It's a guideline, not an absolute law; the books offer more detail than this summary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Opening Image
rubrics_metrics.description: A visual that represents the struggle & tone of the story. A snapshot of the main character’s problem, before the adventure begins.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This should immediately show the story's mood and the protagonist's initial state. The Final Image should later be the opposite to prove change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Set-up
rubrics_metrics.description: Expand on the 'before' snapshot. Present the main character’s world as it is, and what is missing in their life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the Set-up to prepare the reader/viewer for what's to come; introduce key characters and the protagonist's initial goal or lack. The Theme Stated typically occurs during the Set-up (first act).

rubrics_metrics.name: Theme Stated
rubrics_metrics.description: (happens during the Set-up) — What your story is about; the message, the truth. Usually, it is spoken to the main character or in their presence, but they don’t understand the truth…not until they have some personal experience and context to support it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Place a line or moment early that hints at the thematic truth. It often won't be understood by the protagonist until later; placement is flexible (commonly anywhere in the first act).

rubrics_metrics.name: Catalyst
rubrics_metrics.description: The moment where life as it is changes. It is the telegram, the act of catching your loved-one cheating, allowing a monster onboard the ship, meeting the true love of your life, etc. The 'before' world is no more, change is underway.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the inciting event — the first big event that propels the protagonist toward action. Blake uses Catalyst to mean the first BIG event that spurs transformation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Debate
rubrics_metrics.description: But change is scary and for a moment, or a brief number of moments, the main character doubts the journey they must take. Can I face this challenge? Do I have what it takes? Should I go at all? It is the last chance for the hero to chicken out.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Debate to show internal conflict and the development of the protagonist's goal; it's the emotional reaction to the Catalyst and sets up Choosing Act Two.

rubrics_metrics.name: Break Into Two (Choosing Act Two)
rubrics_metrics.description: The main character makes a choice and the journey begins. We leave the 'Thesis' world and enter the upside-down, opposite world of Act Two.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a turning point where the protagonist commits to action and crosses into a new situation (the 'upside-down' world) where rules differ and growth begins.

rubrics_metrics.name: B Story
rubrics_metrics.description: This is when there’s a discussion about the Theme – the nugget of truth. Usually, this discussion is between the main character and the love interest. So, the B Story is usually called the 'love story'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat the B Story as the thematic subplot that provides emotional context and often delivers the thematic insight that helps resolve Act Three; it need not literally be a romance (it can be a friendship, partnership, mentor relationship, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: The Promise of the Premise (Fun & Games)
rubrics_metrics.description: This is when Craig Thompson’s relationship with Raina blooms, when Indiana Jones tries to beat the Nazis to the Lost Ark, when the detective finds the most clues and dodges the most bullets. This is when the main character explores the new world and the audience is entertained by the premise they have been promised.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Also called 'Fun n' Games' in Snyder's terminology; use this section to deliver on the story's premise — what the audience expects to see. Note: the author prefers 'Promise of the Premise' because not all premises are 'fun' (e.g., heavy dramas).

rubrics_metrics.name: Midpoint
rubrics_metrics.description: Dependent upon the story, this moment is when everything is 'great' or everything is 'awful'. The main character either gets everything they think they want ('great') or doesn’t get what they think they want at all ('awful').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Midpoint is a tonal/structural pivot: it raises stakes and often changes information or the protagonist's approach. Remember: 'great' at Midpoint can later be revealed as hollow, and 'awful' can seed growth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bad Guys Close In
rubrics_metrics.description: Doubt, jealousy, fear, foes both physical and emotional regroup to defeat the main character’s goal, and the main character’s 'great'/'awful' situation disintegrates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Escalate pressure on the protagonist from antagonistic forces (internal and external). This beat tightens the conflict and narrows options for the protagonist.

rubrics_metrics.name: All Is Lost
rubrics_metrics.description: The opposite moment from the Midpoint: 'awful'/'great'. The moment that the main character realizes they’ve lost everything they gained, or everything they now have has no meaning. The initial goal now looks even more impossible than before. And here, something or someone dies. It can be physical or emotional, but the death of something old makes way for something new to be born.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the low point or false defeat. It should feel devastating and may involve a literal or symbolic death; it sets up the character's deepest need for change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dark Night of the Soul
rubrics_metrics.description: The main character hits bottom, and wallows in hopelessness. The 'Why hast thou forsaken me, Lord?' moment. Mourning the loss of what has 'died' – the dream, the goal, the mentor character, the love of your life, etc. But, you must fall completely before you can pick yourself back up and try again.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this beat to show internal reckoning and despair; it primes the protagonist for a revelation or inspiration (often tied to the B Story) that sparks the final push.

rubrics_metrics.name: Break Into Three (Choosing Act Three)
rubrics_metrics.description: Thanks to a fresh idea, new inspiration, or last-minute Thematic advice from the B Story (usually the love interest), the main character chooses to try again.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This turning point arrives from new knowledge (often thematic) and marks the protagonist's decision to synthesize lessons learned and act with newfound clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Finale
rubrics_metrics.description: This time around, the main character incorporates the Theme – the nugget of truth that now makes sense to them – into their fight for the goal because they have experience from the A Story and context from the B Story. Act Three is about Synthesis!
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The climax should demonstrate the protagonist using inner growth (theme) and practical skills to resolve the central conflict; show consequences and tie up major threads through action, not just talk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Final Image
rubrics_metrics.description: Opposite of Opening Image, proving, visually, that a change has occurred within the character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide a clear visual or situational contrast with the Opening Image to demonstrate transformation and the new equilibrium.

rubrics_metrics.name: Placement flexibility and beat-order notes
rubrics_metrics.description: Beats are usually in the same order, but they can be moved around. Especially the 'Theme Stated' and 'B Story' beats. It's helpful if Theme Stated is somewhere in the first act and placing the B Story before 'Bad Guys Close In' is helpful to remind the audience of the emotional stakes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use flexibility where needed for your story, but keep audience expectations in mind. Examples: some theorists call Catalyst 'plot point one' while others call Break Into Two 'plot point one'; Blake uses Catalyst as the first big spurring event.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical usage advice: beats-per-act and 'do what feels right'
rubrics_metrics.description: Snyder suggests 9 or 10 beats per act on a beat-it-out sheet, but if it doesn't work for you, don't force it. Do what feels right.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat numeric beat-counts as heuristics, not dogma. The template is a tool to kick-start plotting and revisions; use it to map and revise rather than to constrain creativity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Terminology preference: 'Promise of the Premise' vs 'Fun and Games'
rubrics_metrics.description: The author uses 'The Promise of the Premise' (Blake's term) instead of 'Fun and Games' because 'Fun and Games' can be misleading — not all premises are 'fun' (e.g., heavy dramas).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When teaching or applying the beat, prefer terminology that clarifies intent: this beat delivers on the story's promise to the audience rather than necessarily comic or light moments.
